title: St Mary's Manor, Beverley c.1950 (archive ref DDX1075-3)
description: (Buy exclusive historic East Yorkshire prints from East Riding Photos http://picturearchivesorg/eastridingphotos) St Mary’s Manor, Beverley circa. 1950s There has always been a house on the site where St.Mary’s Manor stands. It has had a varied history, and previously, in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, a house was owned by the Moysers, a wealthy gentry family, associated with the Hotham family of Scarborough. Situated on the east side of North Bar Within, close to St.Mary’s church, St.Mary’s Manor was built for Henry Ellison c.1803. A wealthy man in his own right, he was the grandson of Richard Ellison, a West Riding wood merchant. The new house had a more secluded position, set back behind trees and a high brick wall, whereas the earlier residence was facing onto the street. It was even one of the first houses in Beverley to have gas lighting installed in 1835, when permission was granted to Henry Ellison by the Corporation for gas pipes to be put down from the street to his premises. The house has passed down through the family over the years, then subsequently let and eventually, sold on again, and now today it has been converted into luxury apartments. title: North Bar Without pre 1867 ( archive ref DDX1544-1-4 )
description: (Buy exclusive historic East Yorkshire prints from East Riding Photos http://picturearchivesorg/eastridingphotos) North Bar without, pre 1867 Once called Without North Bar and, like its neighbour North Bar Within, this street dates back to the reign of Elizabeth I, which runs from the northern side of the Bar until it becomes New Walk to the south of the cemetery. It was called Queen Street and sometimes Pucards Lane, a name more frequently used for Wylies Road. Prior to the building of New Walk, the northern part of North Bar Without was also called Molescroft Lane and was colloquially known as the road to Molescroft. The name derives from outside the Bar and therefore outside the town walls. Next to the Bar itself, is the Bar House. With 17th century origins, it was altered by William Middleton , renowned Beverley builder and architect in the 18th century and again re-modelled by William Hawe, architect and surveyor, in 1866. During in this century it became the home of the Beverley artist, Fred Elwell. title: Potter Hill Beckside junction circa 1950s (archive ref DDX1544-1-11)
description: (Buy exclusive historic East Yorkshire prints from East Riding Photos http://picturearchivesorg/eastridingphotos) Potter Hill, Beckside junction, Beverley circa 1950s Potter Hill, known at one time as Cockpit Hill, was also part of ‘Londonderry’ - an old name for that part of the Beckside area of Beverley. Its name could have derived from a pot market which was held there in the 1800s. The chimney visible in the background on the left hand side, belonged to Barker’s Mill. Barker, Son and Company was founded in 1896. After the First World War it was amalgamated with HF Lee Smith of Hull. In 1921, Barkers and Lee Smith became an incorporated company, operating from Barkers Mill in Beverley. The Barkers and Lee Smith premises at Beckside transferred from seed crushing to the production of animal feeds in 1952, and was the last malting in the town. Note the road sign, only one way to go back then, ‘Keep Left’. title: The Bluecoat School, Highgate, circa 1885 (archive ref PH-1-87)
description: (Buy exclusive historic East Yorkshire prints from East Riding Photos http://picturearchivesorg/eastridingphotos) The Bluecoat School, Highgate, circa 1885. It was founded around 1693 by Sir Michael Warton, Member of Parliament for Beverley and one of the school’s benefactors. It was also known as the Charity School. In 1808, it moved premises from Flemingate to Highgate. The Reverend Joseph Coltman, Head Curate of Beverley Minster, became involved with the school and later was publicly recognised for his services to the institution in 1810, when he was granted the freedom of the borough. Lessons began at 7am and continued with breaks up to 7pm. Subjects included religion, book-keeping, geography, short-hand , history and gardening. There were usually eight boarders and in 1870, ten fee-paying day boys and two girls receiving commercial tuition. The school was closed in 1890 and its endowments used for the re-founding of the Grammar School. The shop on the corner was Holey’s East Riding of Yorkshire Botanical and Eclectic Drug Stores offering a wide range of tinctures, barks and extracts. The sign advertises Gresham’s Insurance Ltd. title: The corner of Keldgate and Queensgate from Cartwright Lane, Beverley c.1900 (archive ref PH5-1)
description: (Buy exclusive prints of this image from East Riding Photos) This photograph, c.1900, shows the corner of Keldgate and Queensgate from Cartwright Lane. Previously known as Southbargate, Keldgate became the official name in 1274, derived from the word ‘Keld’ meaning spring. A stream ran along the back of the houses on the right of the photograph. In the 19th century, a number of tanners had established themselves in the street and their effluent made the stream a health hazard. One of the town gates was situated here. Also on the right are Elizabeth Westowby’s almshouses, erected as new in 1864, for poor persons. Nowadays, this corner is the site of the busy double mini roundabout on one of the approach roads to the town. title: Shell damage in the village of Bray, France, during World War I
description: Though the original caption to this image says the location is Bray, the village is perhaps better known under its full name of Bray-sur-Somme. The village is located about 5 miles south-east from the town of Albert. The top of the church tower has been completely destroyed by shellfire, plus the roof at the other end of the church building has also been badly damaged. Moving up the street towards the photographer, the roofs of the houses next door to the church have also been badly damaged, while only one remaining wall is left of the house on the right-hand side of the image. It is likely that this photograph would have been deployed for propaganda purposes. Though Bray was initially a popular billeting village with British soldiers, it was always a rather dangerous location as it could easily be reached by German heavy artillery - as shown in this photograph. So it soon became a place that British soldiers passed through on their way to the frontline, rather than a billet location where they would go in search of some peace and relaxation. A World War I military cemetery exists at the north side of the village. [Original reads: 'OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH TAKEN ON THE BRITISH WESTERN FRONT IN FRANCE. BRAY.'] digital.nls.uk/74548948
